promptHead: Athlete goal: 5K (Corrowmore Harvest 5K) on Sun Nov 15 2026, 10 weeks out, target run the whole way.

new.headline: Stick to three runs a week and grow the time gradually. Daily running is not the way to get ready for November, and last week's walk-run sessions were well judged, so this week adds about 9 percent more time with the one harder run on Wednesday.

flags.title: Calf tightness after runs
flags.detail: You report calves tight the day after each run, gone by morning, with no pain. If it lasts more than a day or gets sharper, skip running and see a physio or doctor.

answers.question: I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?
answers.answer:
No. Keep to three runs a week with a rest day between each. Adding runs quickly loads your calves faster than they can adjust, and that is a common way new runners end up with injuries.

What gets you to the 5K is more running time in each session over the coming weeks, not more sessions. This week's 70 minutes is the next small step, and each week after will add a little more.

Walking the dog on rest days is fine. It is not running, so it adds no load you need to plan around.

new.analysis:
Last week was a sound start: three walk-run sessions, 6.78 km in about an hour, with no pain and effort between 6 and 7 out of 10. Heart rate stayed mostly in the easy zone, so the load was about right for where you are.

Your legs are the limit right now, more than your lungs. You are new to running, and your heart and breathing adapt faster than your calves and tendons do. The calf tightness you report after each run, gone by the next morning, suggests your legs are still adjusting to the work.

This week adds about 9 percent more time, from about 64 to 70 minutes. Every session keeps walk breaks, so your heart rate stays low while the running blocks grow longer.

Wednesday is the one session asked to work a little harder. The build phase adds threshold-type running, and for you that means longer running blocks at a steady, comfortably hard effort, not fast repeats. Monday and Saturday stay easy, and every run has a rest day before it.

Your faster run segments averaged close to 7:40 per km, which is quick for someone new to running. Running that fast every time raises effort and makes recovery harder, so slow the running blocks until you can speak in short sentences.

Heart rate rose slightly on two of the three runs, by about 1 to 2 bpm. That is normal on its own, but it is the trend to watch as the runs get longer.

After this week, keep adding a little time each week and drop walk breaks as the running blocks grow. Around the week of Sep 21 – 27, take a lighter week with about a fifth less time, so your legs can absorb the load before the next step. With about 10 weeks to Nov 15, the aim is to run the full 5 km without walking by mid October, leaving time to settle in.
